newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. INSISTS ON U.N. COUNCIL ROLE IN CRIMINAL COURT.
newsitem.headline: U.S. INSISTS ON U.N. COUNCIL ROLE IN CRIMINAL COURT.

text.p: With the world moving closer to establishing an international criminal court, the United States on Tuesday insisted the U.N. Security Council have a major role in determining the court's agenda.

The U.S. position, which it termed as a compromise, was spelled out during a two- week preparatory session by legal experts from more than 100 countries hoping to establish a permanent court that would prosecute individuals for war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

The new court under discussion is separate from the International Court of Justice at the Hague, which deals with disputes between nations. It is an effort to create a permanent forum rather than special war crimes tribunals created from time to time since 1945.
Most controversial are the roles of the Security Council and national governments -- under what circumstances they can refer cases to the court and also block a prosecutor from investigating them.

David Scheffer, U.S. ambassador for war crimes issues, told reporters the 15- member Security Council could refer a "situation" rather than the name of an individual to a prosecutor. But he said it could also block an investigation of a dispute currently under its jurisdiction.
Likewise a state could also refer a "situation" to the prosecutor who would then have the discretion to investigate or indict the perpetrators, he said.
But the United States is still keeping its options open on when the court could take over from national courts that have failed in proper prosecutions.
"We want to make sure our courts are given a fair shot at our citizens and not automatically subject to (international) jurisdiction," he told reporters.
"There is a reality and the reality is that the United States is a global military power and presence and many other countries are not," he said.

"Our military forces are often called upon to engage in overseas conflict situations," he said, adding: "We have to be extremely careful that the proposal does not limit the capability of forces to involve themselves internationally."

The majority of nations at the conference disagree with a strong role for the Security Council, which in practice means its five permanent members -- the United States, Britain, France, China and Russia -- can block cases.

"It can enable the permanent members, whenever their interests are at stake, to use the veto power to protect potential defendants," said Richard Dicker, a counsel for the New York-based Human Rights Watch.

Many European and Latin American countries want a prosecutor to have wide powers to initiate an investigation without the consent of the Security Council or an affected national government. But all states and bodies should be able to lodge complaints against individuals.
Another group, including some Asian states such as India, opposes a totally independent prosecutor and believes affected states have to agree before a case can go forward.
"We want to bridge the gap," said Scheffer, in allowing the prosecutors wide discretion despite some initial Security Council involvement on some cases.
"The targeting of an individual for criminal responsibility is serious business that should be as far removed from political considerations as possible," he said.

Hans-Peter Kaul, Germany's delegate, agreed that the council should submit "situations" to the court. But he said the council should not "prevent the investigation and prosecution of cases involving such situations."

The session in a U.N. basement room, ending on Friday, will be followed by two more meetings before a conference in Rome next June to approve complex statutes so the court can be established in the 21st century. This goal has eluded the world for 50 years and may do so again.
